source_refs.note: Chapter 13 exercise (PDF 15-17, printed 12-14), solved: 8 MCQs, 8 short, 5 constructed, 6 comprehensive questions and 6 numerical problems. No MCQ key is printed; numerical answers are printed inline.

blocks.prompt: 13.1 Which condition is necessary for most gases to behave nearly ideally?
blocks.explanation: At low pressure the molecules are far apart, so their own volume is negligible; at high temperature their kinetic energy is large, so the forces between them are negligible. These are the kinetic-theory assumptions for an ideal gas.

blocks.prompt: 13.2 vᵣₘₛ of the gas molecule is 300 m s⁻¹. If its absolute temperature is reduced to half and molecular weight is doubled, then vᵣₘₛ will become:
13.3 The rms speed of the gas at 27 °C is v. If temperature of the gas is raised to 327 °C, the rms speed of the gas is:
blocks.explanation: vᵣₘₛ ∝ √T (T in kelvin). T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T₂ = 327 + 273 = 600 K. v₂ = v √(600/300) = v√2. (Options relabelled a–d; see the note below.)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels the four options (a), (b), (b), (c): (a) v, (b) v/√2, (b) v√2, (c) 3v. They are relabelled (a)–(d) here; the correct answer v√2 is the second option printed as (b), which is (c) here.

blocks.prompt: 13.4 Ratio of the rms velocities of O₂ and H₂ at equal temperature will be:
13.5 In a closed room, there is a gas with pressure of 3.2 × 10⁵ N m⁻². If the gas density is 6 kg m⁻³, what is the effective speed of each gas particle?
13.6 Which statement is not the statement of kinetic theory of gases?

options.text: Molecules are in continuous random motion
Molecules are tiny hard sphere undergoing inelastic collisions

blocks.explanation: Kinetic theory assumes that collisions between molecules and with the walls are perfectly elastic (no loss of kinetic energy). Inelastic collisions are not part of the theory.

blocks.prompt: 13.7 Which equation ensures that a star remains stable against gravitational collapse?
blocks.explanation: The hydrostatic equation ΔP/Δr = −GMᵣρᵣ/r² balances the inward pull of gravity with the outward pressure, so the star neither collapses nor expands indefinitely (13.6).

blocks.prompt: 13.8 What happens to a star when its gravitational force becomes greater than its internal pressure?

options.text: The star expands and becomes a red giant
The star contracts and its core temperature increases
The star remains stable with no changes

blocks.explanation: When gravity wins, the star contracts; the gas is compressed, so its density and the kinetic energy of its particles rise and the core temperature increases (Examples 13.3 and 13.4).

blocks.prompt: 13.1 Do all gases have the same kinetic energy at the same temperature? If yes, give example.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. The average translational K.E. per molecule, <K.E.> = (3/2)k_BT, depends only on temperature, not on the type or mass of the gas.
Example: at 300 K, O₂ and H₂ molecules both have <K.E.> = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J; the lighter H₂ simply moves faster (4 times).

blocks.prompt: 13.2 A vessel is fitted with a mixture of two different gases. Will the mean kinetic energy per molecule of gases be equal? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation: Yes. In the mixture both gases are at the same temperature (thermal equilibrium), and mean K.E. per molecule = (3/2)k_BT depends only on T. So it is equal for both gases; only their rms speeds differ (the lighter gas moves faster).

blocks.prompt: 13.3 If density of a gas is doubled, keeping all other factors unchanged, what will be the effect on the pressure of the gas?
blocks.explanation:
P = ⅓ρ<v²>. With <v²> unchanged (same temperature), P ∝ ρ.
So doubling the density doubles the pressure: more molecules per unit volume strike the walls.

blocks.prompt: 13.4 A gas enclosed in a container is heated up. What is the effect of pressure on gas molecules?
blocks.explanation:
Heating raises the temperature, so the average K.E. ((3/2)k_BT) and speed of the molecules increase.
They hit the walls more often and with a larger change of momentum, so the force on the walls and hence the pressure increases (P ∝ T at constant volume).

blocks.prompt: 13.5 The number of molecules of a gas in a container is doubled. What will be the effect on the rms speed?
blocks.explanation: No effect. vᵣₘₛ = √(3k_BT/m) depends only on the temperature and the mass of a molecule, not on the number of molecules. (At the same temperature, doubling N doubles the pressure, but vᵣₘₛ stays the same.)

blocks.prompt: 13.6 Explain briefly, why it is not possible to increase the temperature of the gas while keeping its volume and pressure constant.
blocks.explanation:
For a fixed amount of gas PV = Nk_BT, so T = PV/(Nk_B). If P and V are constant, T is fixed.
Physically, a higher temperature means faster molecules, which strike the walls harder and more often; this raises the pressure unless the volume is allowed to increase.

blocks.prompt: 13.7 On reducing the volume of a gas at constant temperature, the pressure of the gas increases. Explain briefly on the basis of kinetic theory of gases.
blocks.explanation:
At constant temperature the average K.E. and speed of the molecules do not change.
In a smaller volume there are more molecules per unit volume (N/V larger) and they travel shorter distances between walls, so they strike each unit area more often.
More collisions per second give a larger force per unit area: P = ⅓(N/V)m<v²> increases (Boyle's law).

blocks.prompt: 13.8 How does the balance between gravitational force and internal pressure determine whether a start expands or contracts during its evolution?
blocks.explanation:
Gravity pulls the star's gas inward; the internal (gas) pressure pushes outward.
Equal forces: hydrostatic equilibrium, the star is stable.
Gravity > internal pressure: the star contracts and its core gets denser and hotter.
Internal pressure > gravity: the star expands (e.g. into a red giant).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "a start"; it means "a star".

blocks.prompt: 13.1 What will be the kinetic energy near absolute zero? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
The average translational K.E. of the molecules is <K.E.> = (3/2)k_BT, i.e. it is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.
As T → 0 K, <K.E.> → 0: the molecules almost stop moving, so they hardly strike the walls and the pressure of the gas also falls almost to zero.
In practice every real gas liquefies or solidifies before reaching absolute zero, and quantum physics leaves a tiny minimum (zero-point) energy (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: 13.2 What is the average kinetic energy of the oxygen and nitrogen molecules in a room at room temperature?
blocks.explanation:
Both gases are at the same temperature, so both have the same average K.E. per molecule:
<K.E.> = (3/2)k_BT
At room temperature T = 300 K:
<K.E.> = 1.5 × (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹) × 300 K = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J (about 0.039 eV)
The K.E. is equal, but the rms speeds differ: the lighter N₂ (28 u) moves faster than O₂ (32 u), about 515 m s⁻¹ and 481 m s⁻¹ at 25 °C (Example 13.2).

blocks.prompt: 13.3 Consider a gas enclosed in a sealed container. By what factor does the gas temperature change if: (a) the volume and pressure are both doubled? (b) the volume is halved and the pressure is tripled?
blocks.explanation:
In a sealed container N is fixed, so PV = Nk_BT gives T ∝ PV, i.e. T₂/T₁ = (P₂V₂)/(P₁V₁).
(a) T₂/T₁ = (2P)(2V)/(PV) = 4: the temperature becomes 4 times.
(b) T₂/T₁ = (3P)(V/2)/(PV) = 3/2: the temperature becomes 1.5 times.

blocks.prompt: 13.4 Is it possible to boil water at room temperature without heating? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. Water boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the pressure above it. At room temperature the molecules have a range of speeds; the fastest ones escape from the surface, giving a small vapour pressure (about 3 kPa at 25 °C).
If the air above the water is pumped out (e.g. in a bell jar with a vacuum pump) until the pressure falls to this value, bubbles of vapour form throughout the liquid and the water boils at room temperature without heating.
As the fast molecules escape, the average K.E. of the rest falls, so the water also cools. (Boiling point and vapour pressure go slightly beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: 13.5 Explain how the drop of ink in a beaker containing water will behave.
blocks.explanation:
The ink drop slowly spreads out by itself until the whole water has a uniform colour; this is diffusion.
Reason (kinetic theory / Brownian motion): water molecules are in continuous random motion and keep colliding with the ink particles from all sides, so the ink particles move in random zig-zag paths.
As a result the ink moves from the region of high concentration to low concentration. In hot water the molecules move faster, so the ink spreads faster.

blocks.prompt: 13.1 Derive the expression of pressure exerted by the gas on the walls of the container.
blocks.explanation:
Consider N molecules of a gas, each of mass m, in a cubical box of side L (volume V = L³). Assume the kinetic-theory postulates: molecules in random motion, elastic collisions, no forces except during collisions.
1. Momentum change in one collision: a molecule with x-component of velocity vₓ strikes the wall perpendicular to x and rebounds with −vₓ.
Δp = −mvₓ − (mvₓ) = −2mvₓ
The wall receives momentum +2mvₓ.
2. Time between collisions with the same wall: the molecule travels 2L (to the opposite wall and back), so Δt = 2L/vₓ.
3. Force by one molecule (Newton's second law):
F = |Δp|/Δt = 2mvₓ/(2L/vₓ) = mvₓ²/L
4. Pressure by one molecule: P = F/L² = mvₓ²/L³ = mvₓ²/V
5. All N molecules:
P = (m/V)(v₁ₓ² + v₂ₓ² + … + v_Nₓ²) = (Nm/V)<vₓ²>
where <vₓ²> = (v₁ₓ² + v₂ₓ² + … + v_Nₓ²)/N is the mean square velocity along x (we square before averaging because the average of vₓ itself is zero).
6. Random motion: <v²> = <vₓ²> + <v_y²> + <v_z²> = 3<vₓ²>, so <vₓ²> = <v²>/3.
7. Therefore
P = (1/3)(N/V)m<v²>  or  PV = (1/3)Nm<v²>
8. In terms of density ρ = Nm/V:
P = (1/3)ρ<v²>
9. In terms of kinetic energy: P = (2/3)(N/V)<½mv²> = (2/3)N₀<K.E.>, where N₀ = N/V is the number of molecules per unit volume.
So the pressure of a gas is proportional to the number of molecules per unit volume and to their average translational kinetic energy.

blocks.prompt: 13.2 Write the expression for rms speed, and most probable speed of a gas molecule.
blocks.explanation:
rms speed: the square root of the mean of the squares of the molecular speeds.
vᵣₘₛ = √<v²> = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M) = √(3P/ρ)
where k_B is Boltzmann's constant, m the mass of one molecule, R the gas constant, M the molar mass (kg mol⁻¹), P the pressure and ρ the density.
Most probable speed (beyond the chapter): the speed possessed by the largest number of molecules, i.e. the speed at the peak of the Maxwell speed distribution.
vₘₚ = √(2k_BT/m) = √(2RT/M)
Both are proportional to √(T/m); vₘₚ is smaller: vₘₚ : vᵣₘₛ = √2 : √3 ≈ 1 : 1.22.

blocks.prompt: 13.3 Explain the Boltzmann distributions law on the basis of statistical physics.
blocks.explanation:
Statistical physics uses probability to describe a very large number of molecules. Because the molecules have different speeds, they occupy different energy states (levels) E₁, E₂, E₃, …
Boltzmann distribution law: the population of molecules in an energy state decreases exponentially with its energy. For two levels:
N₂/N₁ = e^(−ΔE/k_BT)
where N₁ and N₂ are the populations of the lower and higher states, ΔE = E₂ − E₁, k_B is Boltzmann's constant and T the absolute temperature. The factor e^(−ΔE/k_BT) is the Boltzmann factor.
Meaning:
1. Since ΔE > 0, N₂ < N₁: more particles reside in lower energy states than in higher ones.
2. The probability of finding a molecule in a state varies as e^(−E/k_BT).
3. At low T (k_BT ≪ ΔE) almost all molecules are in the lowest state; as T rises, more molecules move to higher states and N₂/N₁ approaches 1.
4. Although each collision changes a molecule's energy, the average energy of the molecules at temperature T stays E_av = (3/2)k_BT.

blocks.prompt: 13.4 Describe the pressure role on the neutron star.
blocks.explanation:
A star is stable only while the inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure (hydrostatic equilibrium, ΔP/Δr = −GMᵣρᵣ/r²).
1. Formation: in a star of roughly ten or more solar masses, fusion builds an inert iron core. When the fuel is exhausted, the thermal (gas) pressure can no longer resist gravity; the core collapses and the star explodes as a supernova.
2. In the collapse the core is squeezed so much that electrons combine with protons to form neutrons.
3. The collapse stops when the matter becomes a degenerate gas of neutrons: its pressure (neutron degeneracy pressure, together with nuclear forces) does not depend on temperature and becomes strong enough to balance the enormous gravity. The core is now a neutron star, about 20 km across (beyond the chapter).
4. Because of this balance the neutron star is extremely dense: one teaspoon of its matter has a mass of over 5.5 × 10¹² kg.
5. The collapse also squeezes the magnetic field lines together, so the field becomes very strong; rapidly rotating neutron stars emit beams of radiation (pulsars).
6. If the remnant mass is too large (more than about 2–3 solar masses), even this pressure cannot stop gravity and the core collapses into a black hole (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: 13.5 Show that temperature of a gas is a direct measure of the average translational K.E. of its molecules.
blocks.explanation:
From kinetic theory, the pressure of N molecules of mass m in volume V is
PV = (1/3)Nm<v²>   ...(1)
From the ideal gas law, PV = nRT = nN_Ak_BT = Nk_BT   ...(2)   (n = N/N_A, R = N_Ak_B)
Equating (1) and (2):
(1/3)Nm<v²> = Nk_BT
m<v²> = 3k_BT
Multiply both sides by 1/2:
(1/2)m<v²> = (3/2)k_BT
<K.E.> = (3/2)k_BT
Since 3/2 and k_B are constants, <K.E.> ∝ T.
Thus the absolute temperature of a gas is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules: doubling T doubles <K.E.>, and at T = 0 K, <K.E.> = 0. It does not depend on the kind of gas.

blocks.prompt: 13.6 Explain stellar evolution in terms of the balance between gravitational pressure and internal pressure, and how stellar mass determines whether a star ends as white dwarf, neutron star or black hole.
blocks.explanation:
Throughout its life a star is a competition between gravity (pulling inward) and internal pressure (pushing outward).
1. Nebula and protostar: a cloud of gas and dust (nebula) contracts under gravity. As it contracts its density and temperature rise (K.E. ∝ T), forming a protostar.
2. Main-sequence star: when the core is hot enough, hydrogen fuses into helium and releases enormous energy. The gas and radiation pressure now balance gravity (hydrostatic equilibrium, ΔP/Δr = −GMᵣρᵣ/r²) and the star is stable for most of its life (the Sun is in this stage now).
3. Red giant / red supergiant: when hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats up while the outer layers expand (internal pressure > gravity in the envelope). Stars of at least about half a solar mass then fuse helium into carbon and oxygen; massive stars go on fusing heavier elements up to iron.
4. End stage, decided by mass: when the nuclear fuel is exhausted, the thermal pressure can no longer support the star against gravity and it collapses.
- Low and intermediate mass stars (like the Sun): the outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula and the core contracts into a dense white dwarf, held up by electron degeneracy pressure (up to about 1.4 solar masses, beyond the chapter).
- Stars of roughly ten or more solar masses: the iron core collapses and the star explodes as a supernova. If the remnant is up to about 2–3 solar masses, neutron degeneracy pressure halts the collapse and it becomes a neutron star.
- The most massive stars: the remnant is so heavy that no pressure can resist gravity; it collapses completely into a black hole.
So the greater the mass, the stronger the gravity, and the denser the final object: white dwarf → neutron star → black hole. (The mass limits 1.4 and 2–3 solar masses go beyond the chapter.)

rows: Low and intermediate mass (like the Sun)

blocks.prompt:
13.1 Calculate the rms velocity of hydrogen molecules at standard temperature and pressure (STP). Density of hydrogen at STP; ρ = 8.957 × 10⁻² kg m⁻³. Density of mercury = 13600 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Ans: 1.84 × 10³ m s⁻¹
blocks.explanation:
Given: ρ(H₂) = 8.957 × 10⁻² kg m⁻³, ρ(Hg) = 13600 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻², at STP the pressure is that of a 76 cm (h = 0.76 m) column of mercury.
Required: vᵣₘₛ = ?
Step 1: Pressure at STP
P = hρ(Hg)g = (0.76 m)(13600 kg m⁻³)(9.8 m s⁻²) = 1.013 × 10⁵ N m⁻²
Step 2: Formula
P = ⅓ρvᵣₘₛ²  ⇒  vᵣₘₛ = √(3P/ρ)
Step 3: Substitution
vᵣₘₛ = √(3 × 1.013 × 10⁵ N m⁻² / 8.957 × 10⁻² kg m⁻³)
vᵣₘₛ = √(3.393 × 10⁶ m² s⁻²)
vᵣₘₛ = 1.84 × 10³ m s⁻¹
Answer: vᵣₘₛ ≈ 1.84 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt:
13.2 Determine the pressure of oxygen gas at 0 °C if the density of oxygen is 1.44 kg m⁻³ at STP and rms speed at STP is 456.4 m s⁻¹.
Ans: 1.0 × 10⁵ N m⁻²
blocks.explanation:
Given: ρ = 1.44 kg m⁻³, vᵣₘₛ = 456.4 m s⁻¹, T = 0 °C = 273 K
Required: P = ?
Formula: P = ⅓ρvᵣₘₛ²
Substitution:
P = ⅓ × (1.44 kg m⁻³) × (456.4 m s⁻¹)²
P = 0.48 kg m⁻³ × 2.083 × 10⁵ m² s⁻²
P = 9.998 × 10⁴ N m⁻²
Answer: P ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵ N m⁻² (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt:
13.3 At what temperature will the rms speed of the molecules of gas be three times its value at STP?
Ans: 2184 °C
blocks.explanation:
Given: T₁ = 0 °C = 273 K (STP), v₂ = 3v₁
Required: T₂ = ?
Formula: vᵣₘₛ = √(3k_BT/m), so vᵣₘₛ ∝ √T and v₂/v₁ = √(T₂/T₁)
Substitution:
3 = √(T₂/273 K)
9 = T₂/273 K
T₂ = 9 × 273 K = 2457 K
In celsius: T₂ = 2457 − 273 = 2184 °C
Answer: T₂ = 2457 K = 2184 °C (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt:
13.4 If a gas is at temperature 80 °C and pressure 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ N m⁻², having 1 m³ volume, what is the number of molecules per cubic metre, where Boltzmann's constant is 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
Ans: 1.02 × 10¹¹ molecules
blocks.explanation:
Given: T = 80 °C = 353 K, P = 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ N m⁻², V = 1 m³, k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹
Required: N/V = ?
Formula: PV = Nk_BT  ⇒  N/V = P/(k_BT)
Substitution:
N/V = (5 × 10⁻¹⁰ N m⁻²) / (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ × 353 K)
N/V = (5 × 10⁻¹⁰) / (4.871 × 10⁻²¹) m⁻³
N/V = 1.03 × 10¹¹ m⁻³
Answer: about 1.03 × 10¹¹ molecules per cubic metre (1.026 × 10¹¹; the book prints 1.02 × 10¹¹, the same result rounded down).

blocks.prompt:
13.5 The temperature and pressure in the Sun's atmosphere are 2.00 × 10⁶ K and 0.0300 Pa respectively. Calculate the rms speed of free electrons (mass of the electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg).
Ans: 9.5 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
blocks.explanation:
Given: T = 2.00 × 10⁶ K, P = 0.0300 Pa, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹
Required: vᵣₘₛ = ?
Formula: vᵣₘₛ = √(3k_BT/m) (the pressure is not needed: vᵣₘₛ depends only on T and m)
Substitution:
vᵣₘₛ = √(3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ × 2.00 × 10⁶ K / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
vᵣₘₛ = √(8.28 × 10⁻¹⁷ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) m s⁻¹
vᵣₘₛ = √(9.09 × 10¹³ m² s⁻²)
vᵣₘₛ = 9.53 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
Answer: vᵣₘₛ ≈ 9.5 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt:
13.6 A star has a mass enclosed within radius r equal to 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg, density 1500 kg m⁻³ and radius 7.0 × 10⁸ m. Calculate the gravitational force inside the star.
Ans: 2.94 × 10² N on mass m
blocks.explanation:
Given: Mᵣ = 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg, ρ = 1500 kg m⁻³, r = 7.0 × 10⁸ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²
Required: gravitational force on a mass m at radius r
Formula: only the mass enclosed within r pulls the mass m (towards the centre):
F = GMᵣm/r²
Substitution:
F = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)(2.0 × 10³⁰ kg) m / (7.0 × 10⁸ m)²
F = (1.334 × 10²⁰ / 4.9 × 10¹⁷) m N kg⁻¹
F = 2.72 × 10² m N
Answer: F ≈ 2.7 × 10² N on each kilogram of mass m (2.72 × 10² m N, directed towards the centre).
Using the density instead (Mᵣ = (4/3)πr³ρ, so F = (4/3)πGρrm):
F = (4/3)(3.14)(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(1500)(7.0 × 10⁸) m = 2.93 × 10² m N, which is the book's answer.
The gravitational force per unit volume in the hydrostatic equation is GMᵣρ/r² = 2.72 × 10² × 1500 = 4.08 × 10⁵ N m⁻³.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's answer 2.94 × 10² N on mass m does not follow from the given enclosed mass: GMᵣ/r² with Mᵣ = 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg gives 2.72 × 10² N per kg. The book's value comes from the density, (4/3)πGρr ≈ 2.93 × 10² N per kg; the data disagree because (4/3)πr³ρ = 2.16 × 10³⁰ kg, not 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg. With the mass the question gives, F ≈ 2.72 × 10² m N.
